itens.resumo: A contemporary devotional practice of personal self-offering to the intercession and example of Saint Joseph, popularized by a 33-day method.
itens.corpo:
The consecration to Saint Joseph consists of a period of preparation — most often 33 days — followed by a solemn act of personal self-offering to the intercession and example of the spouse of Mary. The method most widespread today was popularized by the American priest Donald H. Calloway, a religious of the Congregation of Marian Fathers of the Immaculate Conception, in the book «Consecration to St. Joseph: The Wonders of Our Spiritual Father», originally published in English in 2020 and soon afterward in Portuguese, adapting to Saint Joseph the 33-day Marian consecration structure created by Saint Louis de Montfort (see Books).

According to Calloway himself in interviews, the decision to write the book arose from his reflection on the challenges of fatherhood and family life in the contemporary world, and from the conviction that Saint Joseph — historically less studied and less invoked than Mary in Catholic popular piety — deserved a method of consecration as structured and accessible as the one Montfort had offered for the Virgin centuries earlier. The priest, already a longtime devotee of both Mary and Joseph, presents the work as the fruit of years of study of the figure of the saint.

Each of the 33 days of preparation proposes between 20 and 30 minutes of reading and meditation: a reflection on one of the titles of the Litany of Saint Joseph, followed by a more in-depth spiritual text on the life or virtues of the saint, and concluded with the recitation of the litany itself. The journey culminates, generally at a Mass celebrated on a feast day connected with Joseph — such as March 19, the solemnity of Saint Joseph, or May 1, the memorial of Saint Joseph the Worker — in the recitation of the solemn formula of consecration of one's whole life to his intercession and fatherly protection.

This practice is part of a renewed interest in devotion to Saint Joseph in the contemporary Church, reinforced by the «Year of Saint Joseph» declared by Pope Francis in the apostolic letter «Patris Corde», of December 8, 2020, on the occasion of the 150th anniversary of the proclamation of Joseph as Patron of the Universal Church, made by Blessed Pius IX on the same date in 1870. The Year of Saint Joseph extended until December 8, 2021, and Francis' letter — which describes the saint in seven facets («beloved father», «father in tenderness», «father in obedience», «father in acceptance», «father with creative courage», «working father» and «father in the shadows») — became, alongside Calloway's book, one of the most cited references in this period of rediscovery of the figure of Joseph, historically eclipsed by Marian and Christological devotion in popular piety.

Calloway's book, released precisely on the eve of this jubilee Year, became one of the best sellers of the American Catholic publisher Marian Press and is today cited as one of the works most associated with the recent wave of consecrations to Saint Joseph in parishes, lay movements and Catholic families around the world — a devotional phenomenon that, decades earlier, had already received other papal impulses, such as the proclamation of Joseph as «Patron of Workers» by Pius XII in 1955 and the title «Guardian of the Redeemer» given by John Paul II in the exhortation «Redemptoris Custos», in 1989.

itens.resumo: An hour of adoration and vigil before the Blessed Sacrament, linked to the revelations of the Sacred Heart to Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque.
itens.corpo:
The Holy Hour originates in the apparitions of Jesus to Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque, a religious of the Order of the Visitation at the monastery of Paray-le-Monial, in French Burgundy, between 1673 and 1675. According to the saint's own account, Christ asked her to unite herself in prayer to his agony in the Garden of Olives on the night from Thursday to Friday, between eleven o'clock and midnight — the moment when, according to the Gospels, he asked the apostles Peter, James and John to keep watch with him and found them asleep three times (Mt 26:36-46). By prostrating himself during this hour, the faithful person is invited to keep Jesus company in his mortal sorrow, in a spirit of reparation for the indifference of men and, in a particular way, for the abandonment by his own disciples that night.

The devotion is classically structured around three elements linked to the memoirs of Margaret Mary: the prayer of reparation itself, meditation united to the sufferings of Jesus in Gethsemane, and some gestures of physical humiliation, such as prostrating oneself or remaining on one's knees throughout the hour. It is traditionally practiced on the night before the First Friday of the month, thus linking it with the devotion of the First Fridays (already present in this collection), although it is also offered weekly, every Thursday, in many parishes and communities of Eucharistic spirituality.

The institutional spread of the practice came in the nineteenth century: in 1829, the Jesuit priest Debrosse founded the Confraternity of the Holy Hour at Paray-le-Monial, approved that same year by Pope Pius VIII, who granted the members a plenary indulgence for each Holy Hour practiced. In 1834, Pope Gregory XVI extended this indulgence to all the faithful who enrolled in the confraternity's registers, and on April 6, 1886, Pope Leo XIII raised the association to the rank of Archconfraternity, recognizing its already worldwide reach. Then in the twentieth century, on April 6, 1933, a new confraternity of the Holy Hour was founded in Gethsemane itself, in Jerusalem — in the very place where, according to Christian tradition, Jesus lived through that hour of agony two millennia earlier.

Today the Holy Hour is usually prayed before the exposed Blessed Sacrament, joining the spirituality of reparation that also gave rise to the devotion to the Sacred Heart and the practice of Perpetual Adoration, both present in this collection, and it is particularly common in parishes, seminaries and religious communities as a weekly or monthly preparation for the Eucharist.

It is a devotion distinct from, though similar in spirit to, the "Hour of Mercy" at 3 p.m. in the devotion to the Divine Mercy (also present in this collection): while the latter recalls the moment of Christ's death on the cross, the Holy Hour is directed to the agony before the Passion, in Gethsemane, and retains the distinctive feature of being prayed, in its classical form, during the night — a gesture of vigil that literally takes up Jesus' request to the drowsy apostles: "So, could you not watch with me one hour?" (Mt 26:40).

itens.titulo: Consecration of the Human Race to the Sacred Heart of Jesus
itens.resumo: The solemn act by which Pope Leo XIII consecrated all humanity to the Sacred Heart of Jesus in 1899.
itens.corpo:
In the encyclical «Annum Sacrum», of May 25, 1899, Pope Leo XIII announced the consecration of the whole human race to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, presenting it as a symbol of divine love and a remedy for the social and spiritual evils of an age marked by growing secularization, in preparation for the great Jubilee of the Holy Year of 1900. In the encyclical, the pope developed the theological foundation of the gesture: if Christ is King of all men, even of those who ignore or reject him, it is fitting that all humanity — not only Catholic faithful — be formally consecrated to his Heart as a visible sign of this universal kingship.

Leo XIII's decision, according to accounts of the time, was also motivated by the spiritual insistence of a woman religious: Blessed Mary of the Divine Heart (Maria Droste zu Vischering, 1863-1899), superior of the Good Shepherd convent in Porto, Portugal, who reported having received, between 1897 and 1899, private revelations in which Jesus asked her to convey to the pope his desire to consecrate all humanity — and not only Catholic countries — to his Sacred Heart. Mary of the Divine Heart sent letters to Leo XIII himself relaying this request; in a way that was particularly striking for the faithful who followed the episode, she died on June 8, 1899, just three days before the pope solemnly carried out the consecration she had asked of him. She was beatified by John Paul II in 1975.

The solemn act of consecration was carried out on June 11, 1899, the feast of the Sacred Heart that year, with the recitation of a specific formula in Rome and the instruction, given by Leo XIII to all the bishops of the world, that the same act be repeated in the cathedrals and parish churches of their dioceses on the same date — making the consecration of 1899 one of the gestures of greatest simultaneous and universal reach ever carried out by the Holy See up to that time.

It is distinguished, by its character as a unique historical act carried out by a pope on behalf of the whole Church and all humanity, from the daily and personal devotion to the Sacred Heart already present in this collection, although both share the same theological basis: the recognition of the Heart of Christ as a concrete symbol of his human and divine love for men. The consecration of 1899 is remembered today, alongside the consecrations of the world and of Russia to the Immaculate Heart of Mary made by Pius XII in 1942 and by later popes (see the corresponding entry), as one of the great moments of the papal magisterium in which the Church turned solemnly toward all of humanity.

Leo XIII himself determined that the consecration formula of 1899 be recited annually, on the feast day of the Sacred Heart, in all the churches of the world — a practice that was maintained for decades and helped keep the memory of the act alive among the faithful long after the pope's death in 1903. Years later, in 1956, Pope Pius XII would take up and deepen the same theme in his encyclical «Haurietis Aquas», already mentioned in the entry on the devotion to the Sacred Heart in this collection, placing the consecration of 1899 within a continuous line of papal magisterium on the theological meaning of the Heart of Christ.

itens.titulo: Devotion to the Infant Jesus of Prague
itens.resumo: Devotion centered on a small wax-covered wooden statue of the Child Jesus, of Spanish origin, donated in 1628 to a Carmelite convent in Prague and today venerated in the Church of Our Lady of Victory.
itens.corpo:
The statue of the Infant Jesus of Prague is, according to historical sources, a wooden image covered in wax, about 48 centimeters tall, representing the Child Jesus dressed as a prince, with his right hand raised in blessing and his left holding a globe surmounted by the cross ("globus cruciger"). Of Spanish origin and uncertain date — attributed by different traditions to the 14th century or, more commonly, to the 16th century — it first appeared in Bohemia in 1556, brought by María Manrique de Lara y Mendoza, a lady of the Spanish nobility, when she married the Bohemian nobleman Vratislav II of Pernštejn. An old legend of the Lobkowicz family claims that the piece belonged to Saint Teresa of Ávila — a pious hypothesis that has not been proven, but is consistent with the fact that the statue resembles those of the Child Jesus venerated by Saint Teresa and Saint John of the Cross. The image then passed by inheritance to Polyxena of Lobkowicz (1566-1642), who received it from her mother as a wedding gift.

In 1628, already a widow and without numerous direct heirs, Polyxena donated the image to the Discalced Carmelite friars of Prague, newly established in the Church of Our Lady of Victory, in the Malá Strana district. According to the tradition of the order, when handing it over, the princess is said to have told the religious: "Venerable Fathers, I bring you my most precious possession. Honor this image and you will never lack anything." The Carmelites placed it in the novitiate chapel, where the young religious made their vows before it, offering it devotion twice a day. Emperor Ferdinand II of the House of Habsburg is said to have contributed the equivalent of 2,000 florins and a monthly allowance for the support of the cult.

The image's history suffered a serious blow during the Thirty Years' War. On November 15, 1631, Protestant Saxon troops took Prague; the Carmelites were expelled and the convent was plundered, and the statue was thrown, damaged, among the rubble behind the altar, with both hands broken. Only in 1637 were the Carmelites able to return to the city; among them was Father Cyril of the Mother of God, a native of Luxembourg (died 1675), who, remembering the devotion of his novitiate days, found the image among the debris. According to the traditional account of the order, while praying before the mutilated statue, Father Cyril heard the words: "Have pity on me and I will have pity on you. Give me hands and I will give you peace. The more you honor me, the more I will bless you." He himself arranged for the restoration of the image's hands and returned it to public veneration. In April 1639, when a Swedish army began a new siege of Prague, the inhabitants ran to the shrine of the Child Jesus; when the besiegers withdrew, which was attributed to the intercession of the image, the devotion gained new momentum.

Count Bernard Ignatius of Martinic, Grand Marshal of Bohemia, offered the statue a gold crown studded with precious stones, presented on January 14, 1651, during a procession that carried the image to the Church of Our Lady of Victory. Years later, on April 4, 1655, the image was solemnly crowned by Monsignor Joseph Corti (Josef Corta), auxiliary bishop of Prague, who represented Cardinal Harrach, then ill. This episode is remembered annually at a festive Mass, celebrated in the Ascensiontide season, on the occasion of the feast of the Infant Jesus of Prague.

Reports of graces and healings attributed to his intercession spread the devotion throughout Europe and then throughout the world, above all through the work of the Discalced Carmelites, making it one of the most widely reproduced representations of the Child Jesus in Catholic homes and churches. The original statue, kept to this day in the Church of Our Lady of Victory, is ritually cared for, cleaned and dressed by the Carmelite sisters in one of the roughly one hundred mantles donated by the faithful; in September 2009, during an apostolic journey to the Czech Republic, Pope Benedict XVI visited that church and presented the image with a gold crown. Copies and replicas of the image are venerated today in shrines in several countries, including Brazil.

itens.resumo: A tradition of dedicating the whole month of May to special tributes to the Virgin Mary, with the daily Rosary and the crowning of images.
itens.corpo:
The first references to an entire month dedicated to the Mother of Jesus go back to the twelfth century, in the Eastern Church, where this month was originally August. In the West, the association of May with Mary drew on older cultural associations with the arrival of spring in the Northern Hemisphere — in ancient Rome, the month was already linked to deities of fertility and flowering —, but it was consolidated as an organized Christian devotional practice only at the end of the sixteenth century and throughout the seventeenth, in the context of the general strengthening of Marian devotion promoted by the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

In Rome, the role of Saint Philip Neri (1515-1595), founder of the Congregation of the Oratory, was decisive in giving the practice a concrete and pedagogical form: he encouraged young people to adorn images of Mary with flowers, sing praises to the Mother of God, and practice acts of virtue in imitation of her during the month, even composing a small program with hymns and the recitation of litanies before an image of the Virgin on each of the days — the seed of the practice that, centuries later, would become common in parishes throughout the world.

The more systematic theological and devotional consolidation came in the eighteenth century, with the publication, in Verona, in 1725, of the book «Il mese di Maria» («The Month of Mary»), by a Jesuit author, which proposed a structured outline of daily meditations for the thirty-one days of May. The work had wide circulation and was decisive in spreading the practice as an organized popular devotion, and not merely as a local custom restricted to a few confraternities or oratories. From the year 1800 onward, the custom of the Marian month of May became established more broadly in Europe and the Americas, gradually spreading to mission countries as well.

In the twentieth century, the devotion received a significant institutional boost from Pope Paul VI, who, in the midst of the Second Vatican Council, published on April 29, 1965 the encyclical «Mense Maio», devoted to asking the faithful throughout the world to intensify, during the month of May — above all through the recitation of the Rosary —, prayer for world peace, for the needs of the Church, and for the success of the Council then underway, at a time marked by the Cold War. The gesture reinforced, at a moment of particular ecclesial significance, the character of collective intercession that the Marian month had already carried for centuries.

Today, many parishes pray the Rosary daily in May before an altar prepared with an image of Our Lady, and it is customary to hold the «Crowning of Mary», in which a crown of flowers is placed on her image as a sign of her spiritual queenship among the saints — a celebration that usually brings together catechism children in a special way and takes place, according to local custom, on the first Sunday of the month or on another festive day in May.

The choice of May, rather than another month, is also read by some spiritual authors as a happy natural symbol: just as spring in the Northern Hemisphere is the time of nature's flowering after winter, May became the month in which the Church celebrates Mary as the most beautiful «flower» of creation and the one who, by bearing Christ, caused salvation itself to flower for the world — a symbolic reading which, although it is not the historical basis for the choice of the month, helped to root the devotion in popular sensibility over the centuries.
